It is also the religious reason they adopted the theory in the first place.
Instead of using Aristotelian syllogistic reasoning to prove that the world had come into existence, as some theologians did, they used atomism.
They found in the atomists’ theory of the “indivisible part” a basis for concluding that matter is finite.
That conclusion then became their inductive proof for the existence of an eternal divine power that encompasses this finite world, just as the world is encompassed by divine knowledge.
From the time of al-ʿAllāf onward, the theory of the “indivisible part” spread widely through Arab-Islamic thought.
It eventually came to include many of the major Ashʿarite thinkers, beginning with the founder of the school, Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī himself.
The Ashʿarites adopted the theory as a way of explaining the natural world, much as the Muʿtazilites had done.
Their purpose was to provide a rational proof that the world had come into existence.
At the same time, this would prove that nature had been created from outside itself, and that its Creator—God—existed eternally.
Here we see the common foundation underlying both Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite thought.
Both begin from the same Islamic starting point.
The Ashʿarites believe that the natural world is made up of substances and accidents.
The substances themselves do not change. They are the things in which accidents occur.
The accidents are the source of the changes, or qualities, that appear in the substances.
The indivisible parts are the substances.
The accidents are the events or qualities that occur in them.
Different natural things come into existence when these accidents occur in substances, parts, or atoms.
One fixed feature of the atoms is that they have no size and that there is no connection or direct contact between them.
This follows from the Ashʿarite view that an accident can exist only in a single individual substance that is separate from all others and exists independently.
Indeed, even one accident that occurs in a particular substance cannot itself exist in another accident of the same kind.

This belief—that substances are separate from one another, that there is no direct connection or contact between them, and that the same accident is never literally repeated—leads the Ashʿarites to deny that universals exist outside the mind.
For them, universals exist only in thought. Outside the mind, only individual things exist.

The reason is this: if an accident exists only in an independent substance completely separate from every other substance, with no relation of action and reaction between them, and if one accident cannot exist through another accident, then nothing universal can exist outside the mind and be shared by more than one substance.
Nor, of course, can universals exist inside individual things as universals once those things have become particular individuals.
So there are only two basic categories through which we can think about things that actually exist outside the mind: substance and accident, or quality.
The other familiar categories—such as quantity, position, action, and being acted upon—have no objective existence in the external world.
They exist only in the mind as assumptions.
In other words, the relations we add to things and call categories are only mental relations. They do not exist outside the mind.
Put differently, they are purely mental operations with nothing corresponding to them in the objective world outside us.

For al-Ashʿarī and his followers, atoms also have no lasting existence in either space or time, because they are “events with no extension and no dimensions,” much as al-ʿAllāf had imagined them earlier.
Space, then, is simply a collection of separate atoms.
Time likewise consists of separate moments, with an interval between each pair.
The same is true of motion.
Like time and space, motion is divided into parts that have no extension, and each individual movement is separated from the next by a period of rest.
If the period of rest is short, the movement appears fast.
If the period of rest is long, the movement appears slow.
So in itself there is no difference between slow motion and fast motion. The difference lies only in whether the periods of rest are long or short.
The Ashʿarites also adopted the theory of the “leap” to explain motion.
They said that motion consists of a leap from one point to another.
They therefore also held that time moves by a kind of leap from one moment to another through the empty space in which substances, or atoms, move.
According to many historians of the Islamic schools, Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām was the first Muʿtazilite or Ashʿarite thinker to adopt this theory of the leap.
We will return later to al-Naẓẓām’s theory of the leap and to his position on atomism.

Because atoms are entirely distinct and separate from one another, and because they have no lasting existence in time any more than they have lasting existence in space, al-Ashʿarī held that an accident:
“does not remain for two times or two moments.”
In other words, an accident lasts for only one indivisible part of time: the present moment.
There is therefore no single unit that continues and repeats itself through time.
The accident that belongs to a substance at one moment is not literally the same accident that belongs to it at another moment, or that belongs to another substance.
For this reason, an accident can exist only within a single moment of time.
The logical conclusion al-Ashʿarī draws from this account of the natural world is that atoms, or substances, are the places in which changing accidents occur.
They therefore change because they are the bearers of change, both within themselves and outside themselves.
And anything that changes cannot be eternal, because what is eternal does not change.
It must therefore have come into existence.
If this world came into existence, then it must have been brought into existence by a Creator who acts by choice and has power over everything.
But al-Ashʿarī believes that reaching this conclusion requires another step.
First, he rejects the idea that a “natural cause” created the world.
If creation were attributed to a “natural cause,” then the Creator would be stripped of knowledge, power, will, life, and the other divine attributes that Sunni Muslims agree belong to God.
Second, he rejects Aristotle’s idea of the “unmoved first mover.”
This idea too, in his view, strips the Creator of divine attributes.
The Creator must therefore be understood as a God who chooses and has power over everything—not as a natural cause and not as an “unmoved first mover.”
Only in this way can the whole world be embraced by God’s power and by His infinite knowledge and will.
At first sight, this conclusion about divine creation may seem to be shared by both the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites.
But Ashʿarite thought goes beyond this common ground in one important respect.
Al-Ashʿarī holds that God continually recreates the individual parts that make up the material world—that is, substances and accidents.
God first creates these parts, then they cease to exist, and He creates them again, and so on without interruption.
The real meaning of this view is that the existence of a thing at one moment does not necessarily require its existence either in the immediately preceding moment or in the immediately following one.
So even if we observe a succession of things appearing one after another, this does not prove that they form a single continuous world, even though that is how things appear to us.
What looks to us like a chain of cause and effect between things and events has another explanation.
God has chosen to create things in this sequence as a matter of custom, according to a will whose hidden reason we cannot know.
Because this sequence occurs regularly, we imagine that one thing causes another.
But according to this view, that is not what actually happens.
It is simply the custom according to which God has chosen to create things, for a wisdom hidden from us.
Al-Ashʿarī therefore believes that everything whose existence is merely possible depends directly on God for its existence, with no chain of causes standing between created things.
He denies that events are causally connected.
What looks like a connection between them comes only from God’s custom of creating one thing after another.
We are used, for example, to seeing burning occur after something touches fire.
So it appears to us that the fire causes the burning.
But on this view, the burning is created directly by God, independently of His creation of the fire.
God has simply established the custom that one follows the other.
From this position, al-Ashʿarī concludes that God, because He has power over everything, can cause contact with fire without burning, and can cause burning without contact with fire.
If this happens, it does not violate the law of divine creation.
It merely breaks the usual pattern to which we have become accustomed.
This position clearly leads its supporters to deny the law of causality in the universe.
Yet causality is the objective law that defines the real relationship between necessity and chance in nature and society.
The same position also leads to the denial of the order of the universe as a whole, since that order rests on objective laws governing the phenomena of nature and society.
This view therefore moves very far, both in its direction and in its content, toward metaphysical thinking on the one hand and idealist thinking on the other.
In the theory of knowledge, it ultimately makes human knowledge impossible.
If the world contains no stable laws, and if there are no necessary connections or relationships between things and events, then the human mind loses the path by which knowledge can be reached.
There is no longer any basis for rational knowledge, nor for experimental knowledge in which the senses and reason work together.
Even sensory knowledge by itself is reduced to a fragmented and mechanical awareness of isolated particulars, each observed separately from any relationship with anything else.
To deny all these relationships is therefore to disable completely the powers through which human beings sense and understand the world.
Taken to its conclusion, this would mean abolishing science and scientific laws altogether.

Al-Ashʿarī and those who followed him in the doctrine of continuous divine recreation—which denies the law of causality in the universe—do not seem to have been frightened by this serious consequence.
They then reinterpret the problem of knowledge in a way that still keeps them within an idealist and metaphysical framework.

Al-Ashʿarī himself, for example, when he tries to correct his position on science or knowledge, says that knowledge comes after reasoning as a matter of custom—that is, because God customarily creates beings and events one after another in a regular sequence. At the same time, however, al-Ashʿarī holds that reasoning does not itself necessarily produce knowledge. In his view, knowledge is something God creates after the act of reasoning.
The theologians who followed this doctrine put it this way:

God knows all things before they happen. He creates them, and He creates whatever seems to us to result from them. He even creates our knowledge of them within the human mind. What God creates in us by way of knowledge is enough for us. We have no need to know more than He does, for He is the best of those who know.

When al-Ghazālī came later, he adopted this view and accepted its consequences. He used it to answer the philosophers who believed that things and events in the universe are linked by cause and effect.
